decks.title: Coordinate Geometry — Part 1: The distance formula
goals: Find the distance between two points using the distance formula
Find an unknown coordinate from a given distance
Test whether three points are collinear using distances
Classify triangles and quadrilaterals from their vertices
Find points equidistant from given points

slides.heading: Coordinate Geometry, Part 1: How far apart?
slides.body_md: In Chandigarh’s grid of sectors, how far is it from the school to the library — along the roads, and straight across?

visual.alt: Grid map of Chandigarh sectors with a school S at (2, 3) and a library L at (6, 6). A straight segment joins them, and a second path goes 4 units east then 3 units north along the roads.
visual.caption: Along the roads: $4 + 3 = 7$ units. Straight across: only $5$ units.

slides.narration: Welcome to Coordinate Geometry. Chandigarh is laid out like graph paper, so every place has coordinates. Walking along the roads from the school to the library is four blocks east and three north, seven in all. But a drone flying straight covers only five. In this part you will learn to find that straight-line distance from coordinates alone.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Find the **distance** between any two points
Find an unknown coordinate from a distance
Find points **equidistant** from two given points
slides.narration: Here are your goals. One formula does all of this work: the distance formula, which is Pythagoras’ theorem written in coordinates. A note on the syllabus: finding the area of a triangle from coordinates is not part of your course this year, so we test collinearity with distances only.

slides.heading: Distance from the origin
slides.body_md: The point $P(4, 3)$, the origin and the foot $N(4, 0)$ form a right triangle with legs $4$ and $3$.

visual.alt: The point P at (4, 3) joined to the origin O, with the foot N at (4, 0) on the x-axis forming a right triangle with legs 4 and 3 and hypotenuse OP.
visual.caption: $OP = \sqrt{4^2 + 3^2} = 5$.

slides.narration: Start with the simplest case. Drop a perpendicular from P to the x-axis. The horizontal leg is the x-coordinate, four, and the vertical leg is the y-coordinate, three. By Pythagoras, the distance from the origin is the square root of four squared plus three squared, which is five.

slides.heading: Points on the same horizontal or vertical line
slides.body_md: Same $y$-coordinate: distance $= |x_2 - x_1|$. Same $x$-coordinate: distance $= |y_2 - y_1|$.
bullets: Distances are never negative: take the absolute value

visual.alt: Points A at (1, 2) and B at (7, 2) on a horizontal line, 6 units apart; B and C at (7, minus 3) on a vertical line, 5 units apart.
visual.caption: Same $y$: distance $|x_2 - x_1|$. Same $x$: distance $|y_2 - y_1|$.

slides.narration: When two points share a y-coordinate, they lie on a horizontal line, and the distance is just the difference of their x-coordinates. When they share an x-coordinate, use the y-coordinates. Watch the signs: from minus three up to two is five units, not one. A distance can never be negative.

slides.heading: The distance formula
slides.body_md: For any $P(x_1, y_1)$ and $Q(x_2, y_2)$, the point $R(x_2, y_1)$ makes a right angle. $PR = |x_2 - x_1|$, $RQ = |y_2 - y_1|$, so

visual.alt: General points P and Q joined by a segment, with R directly below Q and level with P, forming a right triangle with horizontal leg PR equal to x 2 minus x 1 and vertical leg RQ equal to y 2 minus y 1.
visual.caption: Right angle at $R$: $PQ^2 = PR^2 + RQ^2$.

slides.narration: Now the general case. Go across from P to R, level with P and directly below Q. Then go up from R to Q. These two legs meet at a right angle, so Pythagoras gives the distance. Because we square the differences, the order of subtraction does not matter, and the absolute values disappear.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: two points
slides.body_md: Find the distance between $A(-3, 2)$ and $B(5, -4)$.
bullets: **Check —** From the figure: legs $8$ and $6$, and $6, 8, 10$ is a right-triangle triple ✓.

visual.alt: Points A at (minus 3, 2) and B at (5, minus 4) joined by a segment; the right triangle through R at (5, 2) has legs 8 and 6.
visual.caption: Legs $8$ and $6$: $AB = 10$.

slides.narration: Write the two differences first, in brackets, keeping every sign. Five minus minus three is eight, and minus four minus two is minus six. Squaring removes the minus sign. Then add and take the square root. Drawing a quick sketch is a good habit: you can see the legs, eight across and six down.

slides.heading: Quick check: distance from the origin
slides.body_md: Use $\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$.
slides.narration: Square each coordinate, add, and take the square root. Be careful: the distance is not the sum of the coordinates.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: an unknown coordinate
slides.body_md: Find $x$ if the distance between $P(x, 5)$ and $A(1, -1)$ is $10$.

visual.alt: Point A at (1, minus 1) joined to two points, P at (9, 5) and Q at (minus 7, 5), each at distance 10 from A, on the horizontal line y equals 5.
visual.caption: Two points on $y = 5$ are $10$ units from $A$: $x = 9$ and $x = -7$.

slides.narration: Square both sides first so there is no square root to handle. The equation for x then has two solutions, one on each side of A. Both are correct: the figure shows two points on the line y equals five, each exactly ten units from A. Forgetting the negative square root is the most common way to lose a mark here.

slides.heading: Collinear points
slides.body_md: Three points $A$, $B$, $C$ are **collinear** when the largest of $AB$, $BC$, $AC$ equals the sum of the other two.
bullets: $AB + BC = AC$, so $B$ lies on $AC$: collinear
If the largest is **less** than the sum, the points form a triangle

visual.alt: Three points A at (1, minus 1), B at (3, 3) and C at (5, 7) lying on one straight line, with B between A and C.
visual.caption: $AB + BC = 2\sqrt5 + 2\sqrt5 = 4\sqrt5 = AC$: collinear.

slides.narration: If you walk from A to B and then on to C, and that is exactly as long as going straight from A to C, then B must lie on the straight path. That is the test for collinearity. Compute all three distances, simplify the surds, and compare the largest with the sum of the other two.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: nearly collinear
slides.body_md: Are $P(0, 2)$, $Q(3, 4)$ and $R(6, 7)$ collinear?
bullets: **Contrast —** Decimals agree that it is close: $PQ + QR \approx 7.85$, $PR \approx 7.81$. Compare exactly when it is close.

visual.alt: Points P at (0, 2), Q at (3, 4) and R at (6, 7) joined in pairs; the path through Q bends very slightly away from the straight segment PR.
visual.caption: $PQ + QR \approx 7.85$ but $PR \approx 7.81$: a very thin triangle, not a line.

slides.narration: This one looks almost straight, which is exactly why it is worth doing carefully. The two short distances add to a little more than the long one, so the path through Q bends. Squaring both sides avoids rounding errors. When decimals are very close, always confirm with exact values before you decide.

slides.heading: Quick check: collinear or not?
slides.body_md: Compute all three distances and compare.
slides.narration: Find all three distances. Is the largest equal to the sum of the other two? Which point is in the middle?

slides.heading: Classifying figures with distances
slides.body_md: Every classification comes from comparing lengths (and their squares).

rows: largest distance $=$ sum of the other two
both pairs of opposite sides equal

visual.alt: Table of tests using distances: collinear when the largest distance equals the sum of the other two; isosceles with two equal sides; equilateral with three; right triangle when the square of the longest side equals the sum of the other two squares; rhombus with four equal sides; square with four equal sides and equal diagonals; rectangle with equal opposite sides and equal diagonals; parallelogram with both pairs of opposite sides equal.
visual.caption: Name the shape only after checking every condition.

slides.narration: Here is your toolkit. Equal sides tell you isosceles or equilateral. The converse of Pythagoras tells you right-angled. For four points, four equal sides give a rhombus, and you need equal diagonals as well to call it a square. Never name a shape from one condition alone.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a right isosceles triangle
slides.body_md: Show that $A(1, 2)$, $B(5, 5)$ and $C(2, 9)$ form a right-angled isosceles triangle.
bullets: **Step 3 —** $AB = BC$ (isosceles), and $AB^2 + BC^2 = 25 + 25 = 50 = AC^2$ (right angle at $B$).
**Check —** The right angle is opposite the longest side $AC$, so it is at $B$ ✓.

visual.alt: Triangle with vertices A at (1, 2), B at (5, 5) and C at (2, 9); sides AB and BC both measure 5 and meet at a right angle at B.
visual.caption: $AB = BC = 5$ and $AB^2 + BC^2 = AC^2$: right-angled isosceles.

slides.narration: Find all three sides. Two of them are equal, so the triangle is isosceles. Then test Pythagoras with the squares: twenty five plus twenty five is fifty, which is the square of the third side. Work with squares where you can; it avoids square roots. Name the vertex of the right angle: it is opposite the longest side.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: is it a square?
slides.body_md: Show that $A(-1, 0)$, $B(3, 1)$, $C(2, 5)$, $D(-2, 4)$ form a square.
bullets: **Step 3 —** Four equal sides **and** equal diagonals: $ABCD$ is a **square**.
**Contrast —** Four equal sides with **unequal** diagonals would make only a rhombus.

visual.alt: Quadrilateral with vertices A at (minus 1, 0), B at (3, 1), C at (2, 5) and D at (minus 2, 4), a tilted square, with both diagonals drawn.
visual.caption: Four sides $\sqrt{17}$ and two diagonals $\sqrt{34}$: a square.

slides.narration: The square is tilted, so you cannot judge by eye. Four equal sides only tell you it is a rhombus. The equal diagonals settle it: a rhombus with equal diagonals is a square. In the exam, write a clear final sentence naming both conditions; that sentence carries a mark.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: an equidistant point
slides.body_md: Two villages are at $A(2, 5)$ and $B(-2, 9)$. A water tank is to be built on a straight road along the $x$-axis, equally far from both. Where?

visual.alt: Two villages A at (2, 5) and B at (minus 2, 9) above a straight road along the x-axis; the point P at (minus 7, 0) on the road is joined to both, and both segments have length root 106.
visual.caption: $PA = PB = \sqrt{106}$.

slides.narration: Any point on the x-axis has y-coordinate zero, so call it x comma zero. Equal distances means equal squared distances, which avoids square roots. When you expand, the x squared terms cancel, leaving a simple linear equation. Always check by computing both distances at the end.

slides.heading: Quick check: equidistant point
slides.body_md: Set the squared distances equal.
slides.narration: A point on the y-axis has x-coordinate zero. Write both squared distances, set them equal and solve. Do the x squared terms cancel?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: $PQ = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2}$; from the origin $\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$
Unknown coordinate: square both sides; expect $\pm$
Collinear: largest distance $=$ sum of the other two
Classify by comparing sides, squares and diagonals
Equidistant point: set squared distances equal

visual.alt: Decision chart: find the distances; for three points, if the largest equals the sum of the other two they are collinear, otherwise compare sides and squares to classify the triangle; for four points compare sides and then diagonals.
visual.caption: Distances decide every classification.

slides.narration: To sum up part one. The distance formula is Pythagoras on a grid. Use it to find lengths, unknown coordinates, and points at equal distances. Compare distances to test collinearity and to classify triangles and quadrilaterals, always checking every condition before you name a shape.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Classify a figure (3–5 marks):** each set of lengths 1 + condition named 1 + conclusion 1
**Mistake:** $(x_2 - x_1)$ with a lost minus sign, e.g. $2 - 3$ for $2 - (-3)$
**Mistake:** calling four equal sides a square without the diagonals
**Mistake:** using area to test collinearity (not in the syllabus): use distances
slides.narration: Write every subtraction in brackets so negative coordinates keep their signs. In classification questions, list all the lengths, then write the condition you are using and a one-line conclusion. Remember that the area method for collinearity is outside this year’s syllabus, so the examiner expects the distance test.

decks.title: Coordinate Geometry — Part 2: The section formula
goals: Find the point dividing a segment internally in a given ratio
Use the midpoint formula, and find an endpoint from a midpoint
Find the ratio in which a point or an axis divides a segment
Use midpoints to find a vertex of a parallelogram

slides.heading: Coordinate Geometry, Part 2: Dividing a segment
slides.body_md: A new metro station is to be built on the line from $A$ to $B$, two-fifths of the way from $A$. Where exactly?

visual.alt: A straight metro line from station A at (1, 1) to station B at (11, 6), with a new station P at (5, 3) two fifths of the way from A.
visual.caption: $P$ divides $AB$ in the ratio $AP : PB = 2 : 3$.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. Planners often need a point part of the way along a straight line: a station, a pole, a meeting point. If the station is two fifths of the way from A, then it splits the line in the ratio two to three. The section formula turns that ratio into coordinates.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Find the point dividing $AB$ in a ratio $m_1 : m_2$
Use the **midpoint** formula, forwards and backwards
Find the **ratio** in which a point or an axis divides $AB$
Find a missing vertex of a **parallelogram**
slides.narration: These are your goals. The syllabus covers internal division only, where the point lies between A and B. Everything in this part comes from one formula and the idea of a ratio written as k to one.

slides.heading: What “divides in the ratio” means
slides.body_md: $P$ divides $AB$ **internally** in the ratio $m_1 : m_2$ if $P$ lies on $AB$ and $AP : PB = m_1 : m_2$.

visual.alt: Points A at (2, 1), P at (6, 1) and B at (12, 1) on a horizontal line: AP is 4 units and PB is 6 units.
visual.caption: $AP : PB = 4 : 6 = 2 : 3$, with $P$ between $A$ and $B$.

slides.narration: On this horizontal line, A P is four units and P B is six, so the ratio A P to P B is four to six, or two to three. Notice the order: the first number belongs to the part next to A. Internal means the point is between the two ends, so both parts are positive.

slides.heading: Why the formula works
slides.body_md: The right triangles $AQP$ and $PRB$ have equal angles, so they are **similar** (AA): their sides are in the ratio $AP : PB = m_1 : m_2$.

visual.alt: Segment from A at (1, 1) to B at (10, 7) with P at (4, 3) one third of the way along. Right triangle A Q P has legs 3 and 2; right triangle P R B has legs 6 and 4, exactly twice as long.
visual.caption: Similar triangles: $AQ : PR = QP : RB = AP : PB = 1 : 2$.

slides.narration: Here A to B is cut at P in the ratio one to two. Draw the two small right triangles. They have the same angles, so they are similar, and every pair of matching sides is in the ratio one to two. The horizontal legs give an equation for x, and solving it gives the formula. The vertical legs give the same for y.

slides.heading: The section formula
slides.body_md: The point dividing $A(x_1, y_1)$, $B(x_2, y_2)$ internally in the ratio $m_1 : m_2$:

visual.alt: Table of formulas: the point dividing A B in ratio m 1 to m 2; the midpoint, for ratio 1 to 1; and the same formula with the ratio written as k to 1.
visual.caption: $m_1$ pairs with the far end $B(x_2, y_2)$: "cross" the ratio.

slides.narration: Learn the formula with its pattern. The first ratio number, m one, multiplies the coordinates of B, the far end, and m two multiplies the coordinates of A. It looks crossed, and that is the point: the larger share goes to the end the point is farther from. Then divide by the total of the ratio.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: using the formula
slides.body_md: Find the point dividing $A(-2, 5)$ and $B(8, -5)$ internally in the ratio $3 : 2$.

visual.alt: Segment from A at (minus 2, 5) to B at (8, minus 5) with the point P at (4, minus 1) three fifths of the way from A.
visual.caption: $AP = 6\sqrt2$, $PB = 4\sqrt2$: ratio $3 : 2$ ✓.

slides.narration: Write m one and m two, and say which end each goes with. Then substitute carefully, keeping the negative signs in brackets. A distance check confirms the ratio. A quick sanity check also helps: with a ratio of three to two, the point should be past the middle, nearer to B, and four comma minus one is.

slides.heading: Quick check: a division point
slides.body_md: Pair $m_1$ with the far end.
slides.narration: Which coordinates does the first number of the ratio multiply? Work out x and y separately and divide each by the sum of the ratio.

slides.heading: The midpoint formula
slides.body_md: With $m_1 = m_2$, the section formula gives the **midpoint**:

visual.alt: Segment from A at (minus 1, 7) to B at (7, 1) with its midpoint M at (3, 4).
visual.caption: $M$ is halfway: each coordinate is the average of the end coordinates.

slides.narration: The midpoint is the special case where the ratio is one to one. Each coordinate is simply the average of the two ends. Often you know the midpoint and one end and need the other. Then double the midpoint and subtract the known end. This backward use is very common in exam questions.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: points of trisection
slides.body_md: Find the points that divide $A(2, -3)$ and $B(11, 9)$ into three equal parts.
bullets: **Step 3 —** The points of trisection are $(5, 1)$ and $(8, 5)$.

visual.alt: Segment from A at (2, minus 3) to B at (11, 9) with the two points of trisection P at (5, 1) and Q at (8, 5); each of the three parts has length 5.
visual.caption: $AP = PQ = QB = 5$.

slides.narration: Three equal parts need two points. The first is one third of the way, ratio one to two. The second is two thirds of the way, ratio two to one, not one to one. A neat check: each step adds the same amount, three across and four up, so every part has length five.

slides.heading: Finding the ratio
slides.body_md: If the ratio is unknown, call it $k : 1$, use **one** coordinate to find $k$, and the other to check.

visual.alt: Segment from A at (minus 4, 0) to B at (6, 5) passing through P at (2, 3), which is three fifths of the way from A.
visual.caption: $AP : PB = 3 : 2$.

slides.narration: Using k to one keeps the algebra to a single unknown. Set the x formula equal to the known x-coordinate and solve for k. Then write the ratio with whole numbers. Use the y-coordinate to check: if it does not match, the point is not on the segment at all.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: where an axis cuts
slides.body_md: In what ratio does the $x$-axis divide the segment joining $A(1, -4)$ and $B(6, 6)$? Find the point.
bullets: **Step 3 —** The $x$-axis cuts $AB$ at $(3, 0)$ in the ratio $2 : 3$.

visual.alt: Segment from A at (1, minus 4) below the x-axis to B at (6, 6) above it, crossing the x-axis at P at (3, 0).
visual.caption: The $x$-axis cuts $AB$ at $P(3, 0)$ in the ratio $2 : 3$.

slides.narration: The key fact: every point on the x-axis has y equals zero, and every point on the y-axis has x equals zero. So set the right coordinate of the section formula to zero and solve for k. For the axis to cut the segment at all, the two ends must be on opposite sides of it, as A and B are here.

slides.heading: Quick check: ratio by an axis
slides.body_md: Which coordinate is zero on the $y$-axis?
slides.narration: On the y-axis, which coordinate is zero? Write the section formula for that coordinate with ratio k to one, and solve.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: the fourth vertex
slides.body_md: $A(1, 2)$, $B(6, 3)$ and $C(8, 7)$ are three vertices of parallelogram $ABCD$. Find $D$.
bullets: **Step 1 —** The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other: midpoint of $AC = $ midpoint of $BD$.
**Check —** $AB$ is a step of $(5, 1)$ and $DC$ from $(3, 6)$ to $(8, 7)$ is also $(5, 1)$ ✓.

visual.alt: Parallelogram with vertices A at (1, 2), B at (6, 3), C at (8, 7) and the found vertex D at (3, 6); both diagonals pass through their common midpoint M at (4.5, 4.5).
visual.caption: The diagonals bisect each other at $M(4.5, 4.5)$.

slides.narration: The order of the letters matters: in A B C D, the diagonals are A C and B D. Because they bisect each other, they share a midpoint. Find it from A and C, then use the midpoint formula backwards to get D. The check compares the steps along opposite sides: they must be identical.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: a seed-dropping drone
slides.body_md: A drone flies straight from a farm $F(-3, -2)$ to a village $V(9, 7)$ in Punjab (1 unit $= 1$ km). After one-third of the distance it drops seeds at $S$. Find $S$ and how far it then is from the village.

visual.alt: Flight path from the farm F at (minus 3, minus 2) to the village V at (9, 7); the seed-drop point S at (1, 1) is one third of the way from F.
visual.caption: $FS = 5$ km, $SV = 10$ km.

slides.narration: Translate the words into a ratio first: one third of the way means one part done and two parts left, a ratio of one to two, not one to three. Then the section formula gives the point, and the distance formula gives the remaining distance. This mix of both formulas is a favourite in board papers.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: unknowns from a midpoint
slides.body_md: The midpoint of $A(2a, 4)$ and $B(-2, 3b)$ is $M(1, 2a + 1)$. Find $a$ and $b$.

visual.alt: Segment from A at (4, 4) to B at (minus 2, 6) with its midpoint M at (1, 5).
visual.caption: With $a = 2$, $b = 2$: $A(4, 4)$, $B(-2, 6)$, $M(1, 5)$ ✓.

slides.narration: Match coordinates one at a time. The x-coordinates give an equation in a alone, so solve that first. Then substitute a into the y equation to find b. Finally, write out the actual points and check the midpoint. Questions like this test algebra as much as geometry.

slides.heading: Quick check: a missing vertex
slides.body_md: Use the common midpoint of the diagonals.
slides.narration: Which two vertices form each diagonal of A B C D? Find one midpoint, then use the midpoint formula backwards.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Unknown ratio: $k : 1$; on an axis set $x = 0$ or $y = 0$

nodes.label: Use the coordinate you know (e.g. $x = 0$ on the $y$-axis)
Solve for $k$, then find the point

visual.alt: Decision chart: if the point is unknown use the section formula; if the ratio is unknown, write it as k to 1, use the coordinate you know such as x equals 0 on the y-axis, solve for k and then find the point; finally check the ratio with distances.
visual.caption: Point unknown or ratio unknown: two routes, one check.

slides.narration: To sum up part two. The section formula pairs the first ratio number with the far end. The midpoint is the one to one case, and it works backwards too. For an unknown ratio, write k to one and use the coordinate you know. And in a parallelogram, the diagonals share a midpoint.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Division point (2 marks):** correct pairing and substitution 1 + point 1
**Ratio (2–3 marks):** $k : 1$ equation 1 + ratio 1 + point or check 1
**Parallelogram / midpoint problems (2–3 marks):** property stated 1 + equations 1 + answers 1
**Mistake:** pairing $m_1$ with $(x_1, y_1)$ (gives the ratio reversed)
**Mistake:** "one-third of the way" taken as $1 : 3$ instead of $1 : 2$
**Mistake:** taking $B + C - A$ for $D$ in parallelogram $ABCD$
slides.narration: State the formula or property in words before substituting; it often earns a mark on its own. In ratio questions, write the final ratio in whole numbers and give the point if asked. The classic slips are reversing the pairing, misreading fractions of the way as ratios, and mixing up the order of vertices in a parallelogram.

notes.title: Coordinate Geometry — chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. The distance formula
sections.body_md:
The distance between $P(x_1, y_1)$ and $Q(x_2, y_2)$ is

$$PQ = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2}.$$

It is Pythagoras' theorem in the right triangle with legs $|x_2 - x_1|$ (horizontal) and $|y_2 - y_1|$ (vertical). Special cases: from the origin, $\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$; on a horizontal line, $|x_2 - x_1|$; on a vertical line, $|y_2 - y_1|$.

Example: $A(-3, 2)$, $B(5, -4)$: $AB = \sqrt{8^2 + 6^2} = 10$. Keep negative coordinates in brackets: $5 - (-3) = 8$.

visual.alt: General points P and Q joined by a segment, with R directly below Q and level with P, forming a right triangle with horizontal leg PR equal to x 2 minus x 1 and vertical leg RQ equal to y 2 minus y 1.
visual.caption: Right angle at $R$: $PQ^2 = PR^2 + RQ^2$.

visuals.alt: Points A at (minus 3, 2) and B at (5, minus 4) joined by a segment; the right triangle through R at (5, 2) has legs 8 and 6.
visuals.caption: Legs $8$ and $6$: $AB = 10$.

sections.heading: 2. Unknown coordinates and equidistant points
sections.body_md:
**Unknown coordinate:** square both sides of the distance condition. Expect two answers: $PA = 10$ with $A(1, -1)$ and $P(x, 5)$ gives $(x - 1)^2 = 64$, so $x = 9$ or $x = -7$.

**Equidistant point:** set the **squared** distances equal; the squared terms cancel, leaving a linear equation.
- On the $x$-axis take $P(x, 0)$; on the $y$-axis take $P(0, y)$.
- Points equidistant from $A$ and $B$ satisfy a linear relation in $x$ and $y$ (e.g. $3x = 2y$ for $A(5, 1)$, $B(-1, 5)$): they form the perpendicular bisector of $AB$, which passes through the midpoint.

key_terms.definition_md: At equal distances from two (or more) given points.

visual.alt: Two villages A at (2, 5) and B at (minus 2, 9) above a straight road along the x-axis; the point P at (minus 7, 0) on the road is joined to both, and both segments have length root 106.
visual.caption: $PA = PB = \sqrt{106}$.

visuals.alt: Point A at (1, minus 1) joined to two points, P at (9, 5) and Q at (minus 7, 5), each at distance 10 from A, on the horizontal line y equals 5.
visuals.caption: Two points on $y = 5$ are $10$ units from $A$: $x = 9$ and $x = -7$.

sections.heading: 3. Collinearity and classifying figures
sections.body_md:
**Collinear:** $A$, $B$, $C$ lie on one line exactly when the largest of $AB$, $BC$, $CA$ equals the sum of the other two. (The middle point is the one not on the longest distance.) When decimals are close, compare exactly: $\sqrt{13} + \sqrt{18}$ is not $\sqrt{61}$.

**Triangles:** isosceles (two sides equal), equilateral (three), right-angled ($c^2 = a^2 + b^2$ for the longest side $c$, by the converse of Pythagoras' theorem).

**Quadrilaterals** (vertices in order): rhombus — four equal sides; square — four equal sides **and** equal diagonals; rectangle — opposite sides equal **and** equal diagonals; parallelogram — both pairs of opposite sides equal.

*Not in the 2026–27 syllabus:* area of a triangle from coordinates. Use distances for collinearity.

sections.heading: 4. The section formula
sections.body_md:
$P$ divides $AB$ **internally** in the ratio $m_1 : m_2$ when $P$ lies between $A$ and $B$ and $AP : PB = m_1 : m_2$. Then

$$P\left(\frac{m_1x_2 + m_2x_1}{m_1 + m_2},\ \frac{m_1y_2 + m_2y_1}{m_1 + m_2}\right).$$

**Why:** drawing horizontal and vertical lines through $A$, $P$, $B$ gives two right triangles with equal angles, which are similar (AA); their legs are in the ratio $m_1 : m_2$.

**Pairing:** $m_1$ (next to $A$) multiplies $B$'s coordinates. With $A(-2, 5)$, $B(8, -5)$, $3 : 2$: $P = (4, -1)$.

Fractions of the way: "one-third of the way from $A$" is $1 : 2$; "three-quarters of the way" is $3 : 1$.

key_terms.definition_md: $P$ lies on segment $AB$ with $AP : PB = m_1 : m_2$.

sections.heading: 5. Midpoint and points of trisection
sections.body_md:
**Midpoint** ($1 : 1$): $M\left(\dfrac{x_1 + x_2}{2}, \dfrac{y_1 + y_2}{2}\right)$. Backwards: $B = (2x_M - x_1, 2y_M - y_1)$.

**Trisection:** the two points that cut $AB$ into three equal parts divide it in $1 : 2$ and $2 : 1$. For $A(2, -3)$, $B(11, 9)$: $(5, 1)$ and $(8, 5)$. **Four equal parts:** $1 : 3$, $1 : 1$, $3 : 1$.

**Parallelogram $ABCD$:** the diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ bisect each other, so they have the same midpoint; this finds a missing vertex ($D = A + C - B$ coordinate by coordinate).

**Medians:** the midpoint $D$ of $BC$ gives the median $AD$; the point dividing $AD$ in $2 : 1$ is the same for all three medians.

sections.heading: 6. Finding the ratio
sections.body_md:
Write the unknown ratio as $k : 1$. Then $P = \left(\dfrac{kx_2 + x_1}{k + 1}, \dfrac{ky_2 + y_1}{k + 1}\right)$.

1. Equate the coordinate you know to its formula and solve for $k$.
2. Write $k : 1$ in whole numbers.
3. Use the other coordinate to find the point, or to check that $P$ is on $AB$.

**Axes:** the $x$-axis has $y = 0$; the $y$-axis has $x = 0$. The $x$-axis cuts the segment joining $A(1, -4)$ and $B(6, 6)$ in $2 : 3$ at $(3, 0)$. An axis cuts a segment internally only if the ends lie on opposite sides of it.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded**
- *Distance (1–2 marks):* substitution 1, simplified answer 1.
- *Classification (3–5 marks):* all lengths 1–2, condition stated 1, conclusion 1.
- *Section formula (2 marks):* correct pairing and substitution 1, point 1.
- *Ratio problems (2–3 marks):* $k : 1$ equation 1, ratio 1, point 1.

**Common mistakes**
1. Losing a sign: $2 - 3$ written for $2 - (-3)$.
2. Adding the legs instead of using the square root ($3 + 4$ instead of $5$).
3. Giving one value where $\pm$ gives two.
4. Calling four equal sides a square without equal diagonals.
5. Using the area of a triangle for collinearity (not in the 2026–27 syllabus).
6. Pairing $m_1$ with $A$ instead of $B$ (ratio reversed).
7. "One-third of the way" as $1 : 3$ instead of $1 : 2$.
8. Wrong diagonals in parallelogram $ABCD$ (they are $AC$ and $BD$).

questions.stem_md: The distance between the points $(0, 0)$ and $(-5, 12)$ is
questions.solution_md: $\sqrt{(-5)^2 + 12^2} = \sqrt{25 + 144} = \sqrt{169} = 13$. Option (b) adds $5 + 12$; option (d) subtracts the squares.

questions.stem_md: The distance between $(2, -3)$ and $(2, 5)$ is
questions.solution_md: Both points have $x = 2$, so they lie on a vertical line: distance $= |5 - (-3)| = 8$. Option (c) computes $5 - 3$, ignoring the sign of $-3$.

questions.stem_md: The distance between $(a, b)$ and $(-a, -b)$ is
questions.solution_md: $\sqrt{(-a - a)^2 + (-b - b)^2} = \sqrt{4a^2 + 4b^2} = 2\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$. The two points are reflections of each other in the origin, so the distance is twice the distance from the origin.

questions.stem_md: The point on the $y$-axis that is equidistant from $A(7, 2)$ and $B(-3, 6)$ is
questions.solution_md: Let $P(0, y)$. $PA^2 = PB^2$: $49 + (y - 2)^2 = 9 + (y - 6)^2 \Rightarrow 53 - 4y = 45 - 12y \Rightarrow 8y = -8 \Rightarrow y = -1$. **Check:** $PA = \sqrt{49 + 9} = \sqrt{58}$ and $PB = \sqrt{9 + 49} = \sqrt{58}$. Option (a) is on the $x$-axis; option (c) is the midpoint's $y$-coordinate.

questions.stem_md: If the distance between $(4, p)$ and $(1, 0)$ is $5$, then $p$ equals
questions.solution_md: $(4 - 1)^2 + p^2 = 25 \Rightarrow p^2 = 16 \Rightarrow p = 4$ or $p = -4$. Option (b) forgets the negative root; option (d) stops at $p^2$.

questions.stem_md: The triangle with vertices $A(-2, 0)$, $B(2, 0)$ and $C(0, 2)$ is
questions.solution_md: $AB = 4$, $BC = \sqrt{4 + 4} = 2\sqrt2$, $CA = 2\sqrt2$. Two sides are equal, and $BC^2 + CA^2 = 8 + 8 = 16 = AB^2$, so the angle at $C$ is $90^\circ$: isosceles and right-angled.

questions.stem_md: The points $A(1, 1)$, $B(4, 5)$ and $C(7, 9)$
questions.solution_md: $AB = \sqrt{9 + 16} = 5$, $BC = \sqrt{9 + 16} = 5$, $AC = \sqrt{36 + 64} = 10$. Since $AB + BC = AC$, the points are collinear and $B$ lies between $A$ and $C$ (in fact $B$ is the midpoint). Option (d) is tempting because $AB = BC$, but no triangle is formed.

questions.stem_md: The distance of the point $(-6, 8)$ from the origin is
questions.solution_md: $\sqrt{36 + 64} = \sqrt{100} = 10$. Option (c) forgets the square root; option (a) adds $6 + 8$.

questions.stem_md: The midpoint of the segment joining $(-4, 7)$ and $(8, -3)$ is
questions.solution_md: $\left(\dfrac{-4 + 8}{2}, \dfrac{7 - 3}{2}\right) = (2, 2)$. Option (b) halves the differences instead of the sums; option (c) adds $7 + 3$.

questions.stem_md: The point that divides the segment joining $A(1, 3)$ and $B(6, 8)$ internally in the ratio $2 : 3$ is
questions.solution_md: $\left(\dfrac{2 \times 6 + 3 \times 1}{5}, \dfrac{2 \times 8 + 3 \times 3}{5}\right) = \left(\dfrac{15}{5}, \dfrac{25}{5}\right) = (3, 5)$. Option (c) uses the ratio $3 : 2$ (it pairs $m_1$ with $x_1$); option (d) is the midpoint.

questions.stem_md: $M(2, -1)$ is the midpoint of $AB$, where $A$ is $(5, 3)$. The point $B$ is
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{5 + x}{2} = 2 \Rightarrow x = -1$ and $\dfrac{3 + y}{2} = -1 \Rightarrow y = -5$. So $B = (-1, -5)$. Option (d) is the midpoint of $A$ and $M$; option (a) is on the wrong side of $A$.

questions.stem_md: The $y$-axis divides the segment joining $(-3, 4)$ and $(6, -2)$ in the ratio
questions.solution_md: A point on the $y$-axis has $x = 0$. With ratio $k : 1$: $\dfrac{6k - 3}{k + 1} = 0 \Rightarrow k = \dfrac12$, i.e. $1 : 2$. The point is $(0, 2)$. Option (a) reverses the ratio.

questions.stem_md: The point $P(1, 2)$ lies on the segment joining $A(-2, -4)$ and $B(3, 6)$. It divides $AB$ in the ratio
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{3k - 2}{k + 1} = 1 \Rightarrow 3k - 2 = k + 1 \Rightarrow k = \dfrac32$: ratio $3 : 2$. **Check** with $y$: $\dfrac{3 \times 6 + 2 \times (-4)}{5} = \dfrac{10}{5} = 2$. Option (d) is $AP : AB$, not $AP : PB$.

questions.stem_md: $A(2, 1)$, $B(5, 2)$, $C(6, 5)$ and $D$ are the vertices of parallelogram $ABCD$, in order. The point $D$ is
questions.solution_md: The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, so $AC$ and $BD$ have the same midpoint, $\left(\dfrac{2 + 6}{2}, \dfrac{1 + 5}{2}\right) = (4, 3)$. Then $D = (2 \times 4 - 5, 2 \times 3 - 2) = (3, 4)$. Option (c) is $B + C - A$, which gives parallelogram $ABDC$ instead; option (a) is the centre.

questions.stem_md: The point of trisection of the segment joining $A(-3, 6)$ and $B(6, -3)$ that is nearer to $A$ is
questions.solution_md: Nearer to $A$ means $AP : PB = 1 : 2$: $\left(\dfrac{6 - 6}{3}, \dfrac{-3 + 12}{3}\right) = (0, 3)$. Option (d) is the other point of trisection (ratio $2 : 1$); option (a) is the midpoint.

questions.stem_md: In what ratio is the segment from $(2, -6)$ to $(5, 3)$ cut by the $x$-axis?
questions.solution_md: On the $x$-axis $y = 0$: $\dfrac{3k - 6}{k + 1} = 0 \Rightarrow k = 2$, i.e. $2 : 1$. The point is $\left(\dfrac{10 + 2}{3}, 0\right) = (4, 0)$. Option (a) reverses the ratio.

questions.stem_md: On a map of Chandigarh, 1 unit stands for 100 m. Two friends stand at $P(3, 4)$ and $Q(-5, -2)$. The straight-line distance between them is
questions.solution_md: $PQ = \sqrt{8^2 + 6^2} = \sqrt{100} = 10$ units $= 10 \times 100$ m $= 1000$ m $= 1$ km. Option (c) adds the horizontal and vertical gaps ($8 + 6 = 14$ units), which is the walking distance along the grid, not the straight-line distance.

questions.stem_md: Ravi’s house is at $(2, 3)$ and his school at $(10, 9)$ on a map. A shop lies on the straight road between them, three-quarters of the way from his house to the school. The shop is at
questions.solution_md: Three-quarters of the way means house to shop : shop to school $= 3 : 1$. So $\left(\dfrac{3 \times 10 + 1 \times 2}{4}, \dfrac{3 \times 9 + 1 \times 3}{4}\right) = (8, 7.5)$. Option (c) uses $1 : 3$ (one quarter of the way); option (d) is halfway.

(b) Find the lengths of the diagonals $AC$ and $BD$.

(c) Find the midpoints of $AC$ and $BD$.

(d) Name the quadrilateral, giving a reason from your answers.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $AB = \sqrt{6^2 + 0^2} = 6$, $BC = \sqrt{0^2 + 8^2} = 8$, $CD = \sqrt{6^2 + 0^2} = 6$, $DA = \sqrt{0^2 + 8^2} = 8$.

(b) $AC = \sqrt{6^2 + 8^2} = \sqrt{100} = 10$ and $BD = \sqrt{(1 - 7)^2 + (9 - 1)^2} = \sqrt{100} = 10$.

(c) Midpoint of $AC = \left(\dfrac{1 + 7}{2}, \dfrac{1 + 9}{2}\right) = (4, 5)$; midpoint of $BD = \left(\dfrac{7 + 1}{2}, \dfrac{1 + 9}{2}\right) = (4, 5)$.

(d) The opposite sides are equal ($6$ and $8$), the diagonals bisect each other (same midpoint $(4, 5)$) and the diagonals are equal ($10$). So $ABCD$ is a **rectangle** (not a square, since $6 \ne 8$).

questions.solution_md: Distance formula for (a) and (b), midpoint formula for (c); equal diagonals that bisect each other give a rectangle.
